title: What kosher means
hookLine: kosher means fit; some Jews keep the food laws fully, some partly, some not at all

cards: You've probably said it yourself. Is that kosher? Meaning: is that allowed, is that legit?

It's one of the Hebrew words that made it all the way into everyday English. Then there's the other place you've seen it: a little symbol on a box of crackers, a sign in a deli window. Most people have a rough idea.
No pork. Something about meat and milk. A rabbi blessing the food, maybe?
That last one isn't it. So what does kosher actually mean?

teach.b: Kosher, kasher in Hebrew, means fit, proper, right for its purpose. It appears in the book of Esther, when the queen asks the king for a favor, "and the thing seem right before the king." Right, fit: kasher.
It isn't only about food. A Torah scroll can be kosher, fit for reading. So can a shofar, or a sukkah.
The system of food laws is called kashrut, fitness.

teach.h: NOT A BLESSING, A WAY OF PREPARING.
teach.b: And no, a rabbi's blessing doesn't make food kosher. What it is and how it was prepared does. Over the next few days: which animals the Torah permits, meat and milk, care for animals, and why people keep it.

The Torah gives the basic outline; rabbinic law built it out in detail. Kosher food also needs supervision. That's what the symbols on packages mean: an agency has checked the ingredients and the process.
Here's the part that surprises people. Not all Jews keep kosher, and those who do don't all keep it the same way.

teach.h: SOME FULLY, SOME PARTLY, SOME NOT.
teach.b: Some keep it fully, at home and away. Some keep a kosher home but eat more freely outside. Some avoid pork and shellfish and leave it there.
Some don't keep it at all, and some keep an ethical version, focused on how food is raised. In America, surveys suggest a minority of Jews keep kosher at home. That's not a scorecard.
It's a people making choices about something they take seriously.
What almost everyone shares is the idea underneath: eating is never just eating.
It's a choice, three times a day.

how: Jews who keep kosher eat only permitted foods, prepared and supervised according to Jewish law, often checking for a kosher symbol on packaged food. Observance ranges from full kashrut at home and away to partial or none.

o: food that is extra clean and healthy to eat
fit or proper, prepared the way Jewish law allows
food a rabbi has blessed before it is eaten

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: food becomes kosher when a rabbi blesses it
it's kosher because of what it is and how it was prepared.
the word kosher is only used for food
a Torah scroll, a shofar or a sukkah can be kosher: fit for its purpose.
Jews keep kosher in many different ways
fully, partly, ethically, or not at all.

games.q: you're hosting a Jewish friend for dinner and you're not sure if they keep kosher. what's the best first step?
o: assume they don't and cook anything.
games.why: Jews keep kashrut in many ways, so the only way to know is to ask. most people are glad to be asked.

practice: Think of the last thing you ate: where it came from, who made it, whether you chose it or it just happened. No judgment, just noticing.
Then picture choosing your next meal on purpose, for any reason that matters to you: health, kindness, tradition, gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Kosher. Fit, proper: food prepared according to Jewish law, and a word for anything right for its purpose.

orig.note: Hebrew: fit, proper; English kosher comes through Yiddish.

carryVoice: Your line: eating is a choice. Kosher means fit, and it is kept in many ways. See you tomorrow.
